newsitem.title: CHINA: China denies U.S. campaign funding charges.
newsitem.headline: China denies U.S. campaign funding charges.

text.p: China on Thursday dismissed allegations that it tried to use money to influence the 1996 American elections as groundless and urged the United States not to endanger relations.

"We hope they will respect facts... stop these kinds of erroneous actions and not engage any more in activities that will hurt relations between two countries," Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang told a news briefing.

There has been repeated speculation that illegal contributions may have gone into Democratic campaign coffers from Chinese interests seeking more influence in Washington. The party has acknowledged that it received millions of dollars in questionable donations.

The U.S. Senate on Tuesday began a hearing into possible violations of U.S. campaign funding laws amid claims that China had tried to use financial donations to influence 1996 presidential and congressional elections.
"This is totally groundless," Tang said of the funding allegations.
He insisted that China did not interfere in the affairs of other countries.
"The Chinese government will not and does not need to in any way intervene and influence the internal affairs of other countries," he said.

"China has stressed time and again that China has never and will not become involved in the so-called political contributions in the United States because our system of government does not allow this," the spokesman said.
Tang accused some people in the United States of slandering China by "making something out of nothing time and again due to internal political needs".

U.S. President Bill Clinton said in Madrid on Wednesday he would act in an "appropriate fashion" if it was established that China had violated U.S. law, but said no conclusions should be drawn until an FBI investigation had ended.
"I do not know whether it is true or not... however, it is a serious charge," Clinton said during a news conference at the end of a NATO summit.
Clinton has been hounded by allegations over his fund-raising practices for his own re-election campaign in 1996 and for fellow Democratic candidates.
The issue has complicated Clinton's foreign policy moves, with U.S. officials not wanting their decisions to be seen as motivated by political considerations.
Sino-U.S. relations have see-sawed in recent years due to disputes over a range of issues, including China's rival Taiwan, human rights abuses in China, arms proliferation and trade.

On Tuesday, Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican and chairman of the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, began the chamber's hearings by saying Senate committee investigators believe that senior Chinese officials crafted a plan to channel money to affect the elections.

The Chinese plan to buy its way into U.S. politics was drawn up in response to Taiwan's growing success in building influence in Washington and included "typical appropriate" measures such as hiring lobbyists and making diplomatic visits, Thompson said.
